Behind, in front, over, under, chipped

Each miss has a direction. A coach watching from behind the shooter usually says first where the shot went compared with the clay, and only then why.

Behind means the shot passed behind a moving target: not enough lead, or a gun that slowed down. It is a very common miss on crossers. In front is the opposite: too much lead, often after the shooter over-corrected. Many coaches like a miss in front: it shows the gun kept moving.

Over (also 'high', 'over the top') and under ('low') describe the vertical miss. Over is common on dropping targets, rabbits and incomers, and is often linked to the head coming off the stock. Under is typical on rising targets that are still climbing at the shot.

Chipped means only a small piece came off. For the coach it is half praise, half correction: the clay was caught by the edge of the pattern, the cloud of shot. For the referee it is a hit, as long as the piece is visible. Watch out for one rule detail. A clay that breaks, even if it turns wholly or partly to dust, is a hit in both disciplines. A clay that flies on in one piece and gives off only a puff of dust or smoke, with no visible piece, is a miss (zero). In coach slang 'smoked it' means a perfect, centred hit that turns the clay to dust, and 'dusted it' is heard in both senses, so ask when unsure.

Tip: Many of these misses are easy to see from outside. A coach standing behind you sees where the shot went and what your head, hands and feet did. On your own you may fix the wrong thing: a shot behind from a stopped gun is not cured by more lead.

Key points

  • The coach names the direction first: behind, in front, over, under.
  • Behind = too little lead or a slowing gun; in front = too much lead.
  • A visible chip, or a clay turned to dust, is a hit; an intact clay giving off only dust or smoke is a zero.
  • 'Smoked it' is coach praise, not the 'smoke' of the rules: do not mix them up.
  • Fix the cause, not only the direction: more lead does not cure a stopped gun.

Did you know?

A coach often stands slightly behind and to one side of the shooter. From there it is easier to see the shot’s trail in the air and where it passed the target.

Stand Talk

  • Coach Behind, give it more.

    Meaning: The shot passed behind the clay; increase the lead.

  • Coach Just over the top, it was already dropping.

    Meaning: The shot went above because the clay was falling; shoot lower and in front.

  • Coach In front this time, good, now a touch less.

    Meaning: Too much lead, but the gun was moving; reduce the lead slightly.

  • Coach You just chipped it, a little more in front.

    Meaning: Hit on the edge of the pattern; a bit more lead centres it.

  • Coach Smoked it! Same again.

    Meaning: A perfect centred hit (slang, not the rules' 'smoke'); repeat exactly.

  • Coach Behind, but you stopped, so don't just add lead.

    Meaning: The cause is a stopped gun; more lead alone will not help.

For the interpreter
  • Pass the direction on at once: the shooter is already preparing for the next target.
  • Keep the coach's order: direction, cause, fix. If the coach says 'behind, you stopped', the cause matters more: a shooter who hears only 'behind' will add lead, which does not cure a stopped gun.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. The coach calls: 'Behind, you stopped!' What matters most for the next shot?

    1. The cause: the gun stopped
    2. Only the direction 'behind'
    3. Nothing: you saw the miss yourself
    4. A request to add a lot more lead
    Answer

    The cause: the gun stopped

    Adding lead does not cure a stopped gun; the cause is what the shooter has to fix.

  2. A small but clearly visible piece breaks off the clay. The coach says 'just chipped it'. How does the referee score it?

    1. Lost, because most of the clay flew on
    2. No Bird
    3. One (hit)
    4. Hit only if the coach agrees
    Answer

    One (hit)

    At least one visible piece makes the target a hit in both Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting; the referee decides alone.

    Chapter 6 · When a target is scored 'one' (hit)

  3. After a hit the coach shouts 'Smoked it!'. What does he mean?

    1. Only dust came off, so it is lost
    2. A perfect, centred hit
    3. It was a flash target
    4. The shooter should change cartridges
    Answer

    A perfect, centred hit

    In coach slang 'smoked it' is praise for a clay turned to dust, and the rules count that as a hit too. Only an intact clay that gives off a puff of dust or smoke, with no visible piece, is a zero.
